specPoints.text: understand the role of bacteria (Lactobacillus) in the production of yoghurt

primer.text: Yoghurt begins as milk and ends as a thickened, tangy culture, all thanks to one bacterium. This note explains why microbes suit food production — complex molecules plus rapid reproduction — then walks the Lactobacillus process from pasteurised milk through incubation to the chilled, flavoured final pot.

lessons.title: Why Bacteria Make Good Workers
lessons.opening: Microbes earn their place in food production for two reasons: they build complex molecules that factories cannot easily copy, and they multiply fast. Add Lactobacillus to milk and those talents convert lactose into the acids that make yoghurt.
keyPoints: Humans use microorganisms to produce foods and other useful substances.
Alongside fungi such as bread yeast, bacteria contribute to food production.
Bacteria can produce complex molecules, for example the enzymes that turn milk into yoghurt.
Bacteria reproduce rapidly, so the chemicals they make can increase quickly in amount.

low.restatement: Tiny workers, big talents: bacteria cook complicated chemistry and breed fast, which is why food plants hire them.
low.analogy: A workforce of millions of microscopic chefs who double their team every hour.
low.examPointer: Quote both reasons — complex molecules and rapid reproduction — since the mark scheme lists two.

medium.restatement: Bacteria suit industrial food production because they synthesise complex molecules such as the enzymes that convert milk into yoghurt, and because their rapid reproduction lets output climb quickly once a culture is established.
medium.analogy: A bakery whose ovens also recruit new bakers automatically every shift.
medium.examPointer: Name Lactobacillus as the specific yoghurt bacterium rather than writing just bacteria.

check.stem: Which two qualities make bacteria valuable in food production?

options.text: They build complex molecules and reproduce rapidly
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Those abilities belong to plants and some soil bacteria, not food cultures.
Heat tolerance is not the cited advantage.

options.text: They add colour and flavouring directly
options.explanation: Flavour arises from their chemistry, not from pigments.

check.stem: Which bacterium carries out the key step in yoghurt making?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Yeast is a fungus used in bread and brewing.
That mould yields antibiotics.
That gut bacterium is not the yoghurt culture.

check.stem: What does rapid bacterial reproduction achieve in production lines?

options.text: The amount of useful chemical produced climbs quickly
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Reproduction multiplies cells, not their size.

options.text: The milk stays sweeter for longer
options.explanation: Acidity actually increases during culturing.
Fast growth helps the culture, not sterility.

check.stem: Besides bacteria, which other microbes are used in food production?

options.text: Fungi such as the yeast used in bread
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Algae are not the taught bread example.
Viruses are not food producers.
Protozoa play no taught role here.

check.stem: Why might a factory prefer bacterial production to chemical synthesis?

options.text: Bacteria can produce complex molecules that are hard to synthesise artificially
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Cultures need vessels and controls.
Yoghurt certainly spoils.
They consume milk sugars and proteins.

check.stem: State the substance that bacteria added to milk can produce enzymes for.
check.modelAnswer: Bacteria added to milk secrete enzymes that convert the milk into yoghurt.

check.stem: Name the two bacterial talents that suit food production.
check.modelAnswer: Bacteria produce complex molecules and they reproduce rapidly, raising output quickly.

check.stem: Explain why rapid reproduction matters as much as product chemistry.
check.modelAnswer: A process only pays if output scales, and fast division grows the producing population quickly, so the complex molecules accumulate at industrial speed.

check.stem: A dairy wants faster yoghurt throughput. Apply the two bacterial advantages to suggest an approach.
check.modelAnswer: Start with a larger healthy Lactobacillus culture, since rapid reproduction will expand it quickly, and the complex-molecule machinery will convert more lactose per hour.

lessons.title: From Milk Carton to Yoghurt Pot
lessons.opening: Yoghurt production is a temperature choreography: equipment sterilised, milk pasteurised hot, cooled to culturing warmth, inoculated with Lactobacillus, incubated for hours while lactose becomes lactic acid, then stirred and chilled to five degrees to switch the bacteria off.
keyPoints: All equipment is sterilised and the milk is pasteurised at 85-95°C, removing unwanted bacteria and preventing chemical contamination.
The milk is cooled to 40-45°C before Lactobacillus is added.
During incubation the bacteria digest milk proteins and ferment the lactose sugar.
Lactose conversion into lactic acid raises acidity, which sours and thickens the milk into yoghurt.
The lowered pH also suppresses harmful microbes, acting as a preservative that extends storage.
Stirring and cooling to 5°C halt the bacteria before flavourings, colourants and fruit go in.

low.restatement: Clean everything, heat the milk, cool it, add the bacteria, wait, then chill to stop them.
low.analogy: A relay where each temperature leg hands over cleanly: hot sterilises, warm incubates, cold stops.
low.examPointer: Quote the three temperatures — pasteurising, incubating and chilling — exactly as taught.

medium.restatement: Sterilised equipment and pasteurised milk at 85-95°C clear competitor bacteria; cooling to 40-45°C lets Lactobacillus be added safely; hours of incubation let the bacteria digest proteins and convert lactose into lactic acid, souring and thickening the milk, with acidity also preserving the product until chilling to 5°C stops the culture.
medium.analogy: A slow-cooker recipe with strict temperature gates — skip one gate and unwanted guests ruin the dish.
medium.examPointer: Connect acid to preservation in your answer: the low pH both flavours and protects, which is a favourite link question.

check.stem: Why is the milk pasteurised before culturing begins?

options.text: To kill unwanted bacteria that would compete with or spoil the culture
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: To add calcium to the milk
options.explanation: Pasteurising adds nothing.
Water content is unchanged.
Lactose sweetness is not the purpose.

check.stem: At what temperature range is the milk pasteurised?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
That is the culturing temperature after cooling.
That is the chilling temperature at the end.
That range exceeds the taught figure.

check.stem: What do Lactobacillus cells do during incubation?

options.text: They digest milk proteins and ferment the lactose into lactic acid
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: They photosynthesise in the warm milk
options.explanation: Bacteria here never photosynthesise.
Filtering is equipment work, not bacterial.
Freezing happens only at the final chill.

check.stem: How does the rising acidity help the finished yoghurt?

options.text: The low pH suppresses harmful microbes and preserves the product longer
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Acidity sours, it does not sweeten.
Fruit is added after chilling.
Acidity thickens the milk into yoghurt.

check.stem: Why is the yoghurt cooled to 5°C at the end of production?

options.text: To switch the Lactobacillus cells off
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Five degrees chills, it does not freeze.
Fruit addition follows the chill.
Sterilisation happened at the start.

check.stem: State the temperature range used to incubate the yoghurt culture.
check.modelAnswer: The mixture is incubated at 40-45°C after the Lactobacillus is added.

check.stem: Name the sugar that Lactobacillus converts into lactic acid.
check.modelAnswer: Lactose, the milk sugar, is converted by Lactobacillus into lactic acid.

check.stem: Explain why contamination before culturing would damage the yoghurt batch.
check.modelAnswer: Unwanted bacteria would compete with Lactobacillus for the lactose, slowing production, and could spoil the taste of the finished yoghurt.

check.stem: A batch turns out runny instead of thick. Apply the process chemistry to propose a cause.
check.modelAnswer: Too little lactic acid likely formed, perhaps from a culture added before the milk reached 40-45°C or an incubation cut short, so the lactose never fully converted and the milk never thickened.

glossary.definition: The bacterium added to milk that ferments lactose into lactic acid for yoghurt.
Heated to kill unwanted bacteria before the culture is added.
The sugar in milk that Lactobacillus digests.
The acid whose build-up sours and thickens milk into yoghurt.
